title: Shortest Path with Alternating Colors
description: Find shortest paths from node 0 whose edges must alternate red and blue, using BFS over a (node, next required color) state space.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

An undirected graph on n nodes (0 to n-1) has two directed edge lists, redEdges and blueEdges. Starting from node 0, an alternating path is a path whose edge colors alternate between red and blue (the first edge can be either color). Return an array answer of length n where answer[i] is the length of the shortest alternating path from node 0 to node i, or -1 if no such path exists.

blocks.caption: BFS alternates the required edge color at every hop from node 0.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Nodes","0 to n - 1, node 0 is the source"],["Edges","redEdges[i] = [u, v] and blueEdges[i] = [u, v], both directed"],["Alternation rule","Consecutive edges on the path must differ in color; the first edge may be either color"],["Output","answer[i] = shortest alternating path length from 0 to i, or -1 if none exists"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Shortest path in an unweighted graph is BFS, but a plain BFS over nodes cannot enforce the alternation rule, since whether a node is reachable next depends on the color of the edge used to arrive there. This is another case where the BFS state must be expanded beyond just the node, this time to (node, color of edge required next).

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The same state-expansion idea as Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination, just with a color constraint instead of a budget constraint.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a rider at bus stop 0 who must alternate bus lines: red line, then blue line, then red line, and so on (starting with either color). At each stop, the rider can only board a bus of the color required next. The question asks for the fewest stops needed to reach every other stop under this alternation rule.

blocks.caption: Only the correct color line can be boarded at each hop.

items: A node can be reached via a red edge and, separately, via a blue edge, and these count as two different arrival situations since they require different next moves.
Track (node, color to use next) as the BFS state, seeding the start with BOTH possible first colors from node 0.
The first time a node is reached (regardless of which color arrived it), record that BFS layer as its answer, since BFS explores layer by layer in increasing distance order.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
n = 3, redEdges = [[0,1]], blueEdges = [[1,2]]. Seed BFS with (0, needs-red) and (0, needs-blue).

blocks.content: {"headers":["BFS layer","States processed","Newly reached","answer so far"],"rows":[["1","(0, needs-red), (0, needs-blue)","node 1 via the red edge 0 to 1 (using the needs-red state)","[0, 1, -1]"],["2","(1, needs-blue)","node 2 via the blue edge 1 to 2","[0, 1, 2]"],["3","(2, needs-red)","no outgoing red edge from node 2, nothing new","[0, 1, 2]"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: answer = [0, 1, 2]. Node 0 needs 0 edges, node 1 is reached in 1 (red) edge, and node 2 is reached in 2 edges (red then blue), matching the expected output.
5. How Should We Think?

A naive approach might try to enumerate paths or run BFS separately per starting color and merge results carefully, tracking visited nodes globally. This gets error-prone because the SAME node can legitimately be revisited with the OTHER required next color, and a global single-color visited set would incorrectly block that.

The clean fix is to track visited per (node, color) pair, not per node alone. Two separate graphs (adjacency lists), one built from red edges and one from blue edges, let each BFS step simply look up the graph matching the required next color.
6. Brute Force Solution
BFS over (node, color) states using a hash map to only fill in each node's answer the first time it is seen, without processing the queue strictly layer by layer.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n + E)","Each (node, color) state is visited once, E is total edges"],["Space","O(n + E)","Two adjacency lists plus the visited/queue structures"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This version is already asymptotically optimal; the "optimization" below is a cleaner, layer-by-layer BFS that makes the distance tracking implicit rather than storing it in each queue entry.
8. Optimize the Solution

Process the BFS queue one full layer at a time. The layer index directly gives the distance, so no per-state distance value needs to be stored or carried around. This keeps the same O(n + E) complexity but with a slightly leaner queue representation, matching the style used across the other BFS problems in this category.

items: Build two adjacency lists, graph[0] from red edges and graph[1] from blue edges.
Seed the queue with (0, 0) and (0, 1), both marked visited, representing that node 0 can start with either color.
Each BFS layer, expand every current state through the graph matching its required color, marking newly visited (node, color) pairs and recording the first-seen answer for each node.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A "must alternate" constraint on edge properties is handled by folding that property into the BFS state, not by post-filtering paths.
A single node can have multiple valid BFS states (one per required next color), and each needs its own visited tracking.
Seeding BFS with all valid starting states (here, both possible first colors) handles the "first edge is free" rule cleanly.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Shortest Path with Alternating Colors is solved with BFS over (node, required next color) states, seeded from node 0 with both possible starting colors. Each node's answer is recorded the first time it is reached in any color state, since BFS explores strictly in order of increasing distance, giving an O(n + E) solution.
